title: Next-Concept Modeling: 9–31× faster than diffusion baselines
content:
Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) is a two-stage framework for parallel text generation. A multiscale residual VQ tokenizer represents a sequence as a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer predicts that hierarchy from coarse to fine. Positions within a level are generated in parallel, so generation requires one forward evaluation per level.
NCM generates coarse to fine: each level predicts a longer sequence in parallel, and decoding every level shows a sample being refined from a rough sketch to the full output in a few steps.
NCM beats or matches strong diffusion baselines on different tasks & datasets while generating 9-31× faster.
Weights and tokenized datasets are hosted in the NCM Hugging Face collection. Each released model consists of a frozen tokenizer and a next-concept generator.
git clone https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm.git
cd ncm
pip install -r requirements.txt
Python 3.10 or newer and a CUDA-capable PyTorch installation are recommended.
Download the checkpoints and evaluation inputs:
hf download hazyresearch/ncm-checkpoints --local-dir artifacts
hf download hazyresearch/ncm-datasets --repo-type dataset --local-dir data
Then run:
python evaluate.py --config config/eval/<task>.yaml --checkpoint-dir artifacts/<task> --data-dir data/<task>
# <task> is one of xsum, wmt14, sudoku-easy, sudoku-medium or sudoku-hard
python evaluate.py --config config/eval/<dataset>.yaml --checkpoint-dir artifacts/<dataset>
# <dataset> is tinystories, owt or lm1b-<size> with <size> one of small, medium or large
This runs one generation shard per visible GPU, merges them, and prints ROUGE-1/2/L and generative perplexity for XSum; cased and lowercased sacreBLEU, chrF and length ratio for WMT14; solved, cell and valid-grid rates for Sudoku; and generative perplexity under GPT-2 large with unigram entropy, over 5 seeds of 256 unconditional samples, for TinyStories, OpenWebText and LM1B, the latter under the FLM scoring protocol. Add --cfg <scale> for classifier-free guidance on XSum and WMT14; the guided WMT14 row uses --cfg 1.0.
- evaluate.py: evaluation entry point
- scripts/: per-GPU generation shard and the merge that scores it
- config/eval/: one config per released checkpoint, identical to the config.yaml shipped with it
- models/, tokenization/: generator and tokenizer implementations

report.summary: HazyResearch's Next-Concept Modeling generates text coarse-to-fine in parallel over a token hierarchy, matching or beating diffusion baselines while running 9–31× faster.
report.background: Diffusion language models (LLaDA, Mercury, MDLM-style masked diffusion) have become the main challenger to autoregressive LLMs, promising parallel decoding and bidirectional context. The catch is that generation quality depends on many denoising steps, and every step costs a full forward pass over the whole sequence, so speed gains often evaporate at usable quality levels. Because text is discrete, diffusion must also be adapted through absorbing-state or masked formulations rather than continuous noise. Autoregressive decoding, meanwhile, remains strictly sequential. NCM comes from Chris Ré's HazyResearch lab at Stanford, a group known for efficient sequence-model building blocks and hierarchical/multiscale representations. Rather than denoising noisy tokens, NCM reframes fast generation as hierarchical prediction: compress the sequence into a coarse-to-fine stack of discrete codes, then predict that stack one level at a time.
key_points: Two-stage architecture: a multiscale residual vector-quantized tokenizer turns a text sequence into a hierarchy of discrete codes, from a short coarse sketch to fine detail. A transformer then learns to predict that hierarchy. The tokenizer stays frozen at generation time; only the next-concept generator does the work.

Parallel within each level: all positions of a given hierarchy level are generated simultaneously, so decoding needs just one forward evaluation per level instead of dozens of denoising steps. The outputs visibly refine from a rough sketch to full text in a handful of steps.

Speed and quality together: the authors report 9–31× faster generation than strong diffusion baselines while matching or beating them. That range reflects different tasks and datasets rather than a single cherry-picked benchmark.

Broad task coverage: released checkpoints span summarization (XSum with ROUGE-1/2/L), translation (WMT14 with sacreBLEU, chrF, length ratio), constraint satisfaction (Sudoku easy/medium/hard solve and validity rates), and unconditional LM perplexity on TinyStories, OpenWebText and LM1B under the FLM scoring protocol.

Open and reproducible: MIT-licensed code, Hugging Face checkpoints and tokenized datasets, per-GPU sharded evaluation scripts, and configs matching each shipped checkpoint, plus classifier-free guidance support via a --cfg flag for XSum and WMT14.
report.impact: For the AI industry, NCM is a serious data point that parallel text generation does not have to mean slow sampling. If the 9–31× speedup holds across model scales, diffusion-style decoders lose their main practical drawback, and the economics of inference shift: fewer forward passes per request means lower latency and cost for high-throughput serving. For developers, the barrier to experimenting drops sharply, since checkpoints, tokenized data and eval scripts are released under MIT and run on a single CUDA PyTorch setup. The design also opens a new research axis — tokenizer hierarchy depth and codebook structure become tunable knobs alongside model size. For regular users, the near-term effect is less about replacing chat models and more about latency-sensitive, structured outputs like translation, summarization and constraint-heavy tasks such as Sudoku, where fast parallel decoding is genuinely useful.
report.tools: Start with the repo itself: github.com/HazyResearch/ncm, then pull hazyresearch/ncm-checkpoints and hazyresearch/ncm-datasets from Hugging Face. Compare against open diffusion LM baselines such as LLaDA and MDLM/Diffu-GPT implementations, and score with the same harnesses the paper reports — sacreBLEU, ROUGE and GPT-2-large generative perplexity. If you want to go deeper, read the arXiv paper (2610.14162) alongside the models/ and tokenization/ source to see how the residual-VQ hierarchy is built.
